newsitem.title: THAILAND: Baht curbs to hit Thai debt securitisation.
newsitem.headline: Baht curbs to hit Thai debt securitisation.

text.p: Plans to securitise billions of dollars in ailing Thai finance firm's property sector loans will be difficult to implement given current poor economic and monetary conditions, analysts and executives said on Wednesday.

The Thai government issued decrees on Tuesday to extend existing proposals to buy loans, mortgages or assets granted by finance companies to the cash-strapped property sector and securitise them as tradeable bonds or other securities.
But currency controls recently imposed by the central bank to deter foreign baht speculators would make the sale of those securities extremely difficult at this time, analysts said.

The shaky state of the baht, which was last attacked in May as the country plunged deeper into its worst economic crisis in over a decade, meant foreign investors would wish to hedge their currency exposure.
But costs of doing so have soared since May because the controls have sent offshore dollar/baht swap rates soaring as the central bank squeezed speculators.

"Theoretically if you want your securitisation to be successful you are looking at some loosening of the capital controls...I personally don't see much getting done until the capital controls are loosened," said Kenneth Ng, finance and securities analyst at ING Barings.

Technically securitisation, despite high up-front administrative and legal costs, offers excellent prospects to refinance a Thai finance sector urgently in need of recapitalisation as financing avenues are slowly being exhausted or are prohibitively expensive, executives said.
The sector, comprising some 90 firms, is faced with tightening liquidity, declining revenues, deteriorating asset quality and rising costs.

A local industry executive on Monday estimated that as much as 31.5 percent of the industry's total 1.47 billion baht ($58 billion dollars) loan portfolio may be non-performing, much of it the result of lending to a sour local property market.

Since securitisation normally protects investors from the underlying asset quality -- instruments are guaranteed by repayments not assets -- it probably offers the Thai firms their most effective remaining financing channel, executives said.

"It really tackles the liquidity problem directly. The market situation now is one of a lack of liquidity and turning hard assets into cash takes care of that problem completely," said Trakarn Sriamwala, assistant vice-president at Sitca Investment and Securities Plc.
The firm is one of two that successfully sold off hire purchase portfolios to international investors prior to the country's current problems.
But those problems are now holding up a number of planned private deals pending relaxation of the capital restrictions, executives said.
"Currently there are quite a number of deals going ahead but they are halted because of basically this matter," Trakarn said. ($1 = 25 baht)
